The American embargo on Japan in 1941 cut off the oil, steel and other materials that its war economy needed, and pushed Japan's leaders toward war.

Japan's war in China had been going since 1937, and in 1940 it moved into northern French Indochina. The United States answered with limits on scrap iron and steel. After Japan occupied southern Indochina in July 1941, President Franklin Roosevelt froze Japanese assets and, with Britain and the Dutch, stopped oil exports. Japan imported most of its oil, and its stocks would last only a year or two.

Talks failed. Leaders in Tokyo concluded that they must take the oil of the Dutch East Indies and strike the American fleet first. The result was the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 and the start of the Pacific War.
sum: The American embargo on Japan in 1941 cut off the oil, steel and other materials that its war economy needed, and pushed Japan's leaders toward war.
